content: The HIV testing information should be collected in a standardized manner across all service sites, including both facility and community levels. At a minimum, the following data points must be recorded: the date of the HIV test, the test result, the date of diagnosis, the date the client received the result, and, where feasible and appropriate, linkage to care. This ensures consistency and completeness in data collection practices, which may vary across different settings and testing approaches. Since 2017, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that antiretroviral therapy (ART) be offered to all individuals living with HIV within seven days of a confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment, preferably on the same day, for those ready to start treatment. Patient monitoring tools, including electronic medical record (EMR) systems, should be updated to track rapid treatment initiation. WHO has also updated its recommendations for preferred and alternative first-, second-, and third-line ART regimens for neonates, infants, children, adolescents, and adults, including pregnant and breastfeeding women. These updates necessitate revisions to existing drug regimens, patient monitoring tools, EMR systems, and the minimum dataset for HIV treatment. Routine viral load (VL) monitoring is recommended at six and 12 months after ART initiation and annually thereafter. CD4 cell count testing should be conducted at the first presentation to care and every six months until the patient is established on ART. CD4 monitoring is also necessary when clinically indicated, such as for advanced HIV disease assessment or re-engagement in care. Patient monitoring tools and EMR systems should be revised to incorporate these updates. In 2021, WHO introduced a new indicator for early VL testing, recommending a review of VL test results within six months of treatment initiation to promote early ART adherence and VL suppression. Patient monitoring tools should be updated to capture this early testing. The definition of loss to follow-up (LTFU) was revised in 2020, reducing the criterion from 90 or more days to 28 or more days since the last missed appointment, including missed antiretroviral (ARV) refills in both facility and community settings. Systems used to track LTFU, such as EMR and appointment systems, should be updated accordingly. Updated recommendations for ART service delivery include initiating ART outside health facilities, scheduling clinic visits at threeto six-month intervals, and implementing tracing interventions for individuals disengaged from care. Monitoring these recommendations requires updates to HIV patient monitoring tools, including those adapted for community-delivered ART services, and the development of indicators for differentiated service delivery, such as multi-month ARV dispensing and criteria for triggering tracing interventions. ARV toxicity monitoring indicators were revised in 2020 to capture emerging signals associated with new ARVs, including weight gain and cardiometabolic toxicities. An additional indicator monitors adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as low birth weight, stillbirths, miscarriages, preterm births, and congenital abnormalities related to ARV exposure during pregnancy. Patient monitoring tools should be updated to capture these emerging toxicities. In the context of the treat all policy, it remains critical to monitor individuals living with HIV who receive ART over time as they move between health facilities and access care at different service delivery points. Late ART initiation often reflects treatment interruption, disengagement from care, or challenges with linkage to care. Among children, late diagnosis is associated with delays in identifying those at risk of HIV infection and accessing testing. Delays in infant diagnosis may result from provider factors, such as the availability of testing and laboratory delays, or client factors, such as failure to return for testing. ART initiation should follow person-centered care principles, focusing on the health needs, preferences, and expectations of individuals and communities. Monitoring should enable longitudinal tracking of individuals living with HIV as they access treatment and care services, re-engage in care, and reinitiate treatment when necessary. Rapid ART initiation should be offered to all individuals living with HIV following a confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment. For those with suspected tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated while investigating for TB, with close follow-up to start TB treatment if confirmed. For individuals with HIV-associated TB, ART should begin within two weeks of starting TB treatment. However, for those with TB meningitis, ART should be delayed by at least four weeks and initiated within eight weeks of starting TB treatment. Similarly, ART initiation should be deferred by 4–6 weeks for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis to reduce mortality risk. Monitoring treatment outcomes, including viral suppression, is essential. Viral suppression is defined as a VL of less than 1,000 copies/mL. Patient monitoring systems should be capable of identifying VL tests conducted at six months after ART initiation and ensuring this is accounted for in HIV surveillance to avoid disrupting population-level VL monitoring.
